releases.title: Sites can no longer claim each other's servers
notes: This release fixes a security problem in how sites that talk to each other decide where to send your requests. Until now, the first site to mention a server, a channel or a conversation was believed for everyone on your site. A dishonest site could claim a server that lives on another site, and then receive the requests people on your site made about it, even after they joined it from its real site. It could answer in the real site's place with its own version of the server, choose the keys your app used there, and read what people then posted in it. The security advisory on GitHub explains it in full.

Now a site's claim only counts for the person it was made to. Joining a server from its own site, from its listing or with an invite, outweighs what other sites say about it, and nothing another site says moves a server you've joined or a route your site already knew. Ids that apps choose, such as a thread's, can no longer steer where a request goes.

If two sites claim the same thing, your site sends your requests about it to neither, and the app says so. Tell your site's admin: the site's log names the two sites, and blocking the wrong one puts things right.

Messages on the real server stayed end-to-end encrypted throughout, and in conversations the app's checks on who's in them stop a site from silently adding a reader. The risk was to what someone posted in a server while its requests went to a dishonest site.

For people who run a site: please update. Your site keeps every route it already knew, so nothing stops working, and the updater offers 0.24.25 as usual. A route a dishonest site took over before you updated is kept too, until you block that site: your site's log names it when the real site speaks up, and the advisory explains how to check. The hosted site is fixed as well.

releases.title: The hosted site's clean-up no longer skips a scheduled run
notes: On the hosted site, a call to the clean-up's public address just before a task's shared gap ended could make the next scheduled run skip, which for removing inactive accounts meant waiting a day. An instance now only holds a task back until that shared gap ends, so the scheduled run goes ahead. Self-hosted sites run these tasks on timers and weren't affected.

releases.title: Security fixes from the November audit: server pushes only where they're wanted, and a working destination check
notes: Server notifications now go only where they're wanted. With push notifications on, each browser tells this site, per server, whether it wants a push for every message, only for @mentions, or none, worked out from your own notification settings. A busy server no longer wakes every member's phone for each message. The site learns this choice per server; your settings for single channels stay on your device. Until an app has updated, it gets @mentions from every server and other activity from every server except the site's default one, whatever it was set to.

Checking another site before a move works again. The browser used to fetch the other site's public document itself, which the site's own security policy blocked. Now your site reads it for you, with the same address checks as federation and the sites it refuses, without trusting or remembering the other site, and up to 10 checks every 10 minutes.

The hosted site's scheduled clean-up can be called by anyone, as every function can. Now each task starts at most once a minute (deliveries), every 5 minutes (expiry) or every hour (inactive accounts) across every instance, as far as two calls at the same moment allow, so repeated calls cost one read at most instead of a full run. Replies from other sites are also counted as they arrive and cut off at the limit on the hosted site, as on self-hosted sites.

Self-hosted sites: a new section in Servers and voice explains how to keep a TURN relay away from your private network (coturn settings), and the example settings file lost a stray `\n` in a comment. Nothing new to set.

The Rust server's own P-256 code (Web Push and passkeys) moved to p256 0.14, away from a big-number library with a timing advisory. Other Rust dependencies were updated (including url 2.5.9). The server and updater now refuse unsafe code, and a request that fails while holding a lock no longer breaks the requests after it.

Known vulnerabilities in the Rust crates are now checked on every pull request (cargo-deny), and each exception records why it doesn't apply and when it expires. rusqlite stays at 0.37 until OpenMLS allows a newer SQLite: the server only ever opens its own database files.
Follows Secure Net 0.8.0. The experimental account-transfer code now keeps only a digest of the possession answer, never the answer itself. It stays off and experimental.
Base44's Vite plugin is updated to 1.0.55, and the repository now asks every agent and person to change it through reviewed pull requests, never straight on main.

releases.title: Repair silent SNIP proposal sync stalls and safely recover from GitHub cache failures
notes: Fixed the misleading silent no-op when GitHub retrieval failed and the known SNIP cache was marked stale. Missing discussions for main-branch proposal files verified in the last 12 hours can now be posted and explicitly labelled as cached while any stale merge/decline closure or open-PR-only creation stays blocked until fresh GitHub verification.

The authorised admin device now shows GitHub snapshot freshness, pending work and the last successfully processed proposal. Missing server-forum permissions, unloaded encrypted channels, offline mode and locally queued unconfirmed messages produce explicit feedback rather than being mistaken for successful synchronisation.

The background sync remains one signed proposal operation per pass with pacing, rate-limit cooldown, unique message IDs, preservation of the forum encryption model and automatic restart on a later pass. A locally queued ciphertext is not counted as a persisted server post.

New regression tests cover stale-cached known main-branch SNIP-0007 and SNIP-0008 discussion creation without false closure, expired snapshots, open-PR stale denial, missing forum channel failure and no duplicate notes or posts. Updated SNIP forum and troubleshooting documentation with behaviour and safety limitations.

Existing Commonveil messaging, server keys, administrator permissions, protocol governance and experimental Secure Net relay switches are unchanged. Site owners do not gain access to encryption keys. The default server still requires an authorised admin device to actually sign and publish missing posts.

releases.title: Secure Net proposal forum rate-limit recovery and safe incremental synchronisation
notes: Fixed the Secure Net proposals Sync now control overloading Base44 shared backend requests. The hosted snips.status function now loads bounded batches of signed thread and closure metadata using one $in query for the current SNIP list rather than two separate requests for every proposal.

The authorised admin device now reconciles one proposal at a time, prioritising genuinely missing SNIP posts (including SNIP-0007 and SNIP-0008) before older merged-thread closure work. It pauses between changes while the authorised app is visible, keeping forum end-to-end encryption and signatures on the device.

When Base44 returns HTTP 429 / UPSTREAM_BUSY or a transient network error, synchronisation now enters a bounded, increasing cooldown and retries automatically without repeatedly hammering the backend. Sync now changes to Retry queued during a rate-limit pause, and the UI retains an explicit error for non-rate-limit failures.

Removed the redundant second snips.status request after every pass. The interface reports the full backlog instead of only the number scheduled in its current one-step batch and does not act on stale GitHub snapshots.

Fixed IDs preserve idempotent encrypted proposal posts and notes. If a rate limit interrupts after posting but before locking, the next authorised-device pass closes the existing thread without duplicating the post or its rationale.

Matched the self-hosted Rust status implementation to the batched lookup contract. Added regression tests for batching, prioritisation, missing-thread recovery and interruption after a signed closing note. This does not enable server-side access to Commonveil private encryption keys or bypass admin approval.

releases.title: Host ownership, Mastodon-style domain moderation and transparent SNIP closure reasons
notes: Introduced site-level policy distinct from each encrypted community server. The host owner controls registration and federation mode (open, approved sites only, off). Delegated site admins can manage up to 20 public rules, contact and appeals details, local remote-site decisions and publication of public domain block reasons. Private staff notes remain backend-only.

Site administrators can suspend an exact remote hostname, limit new remote interactions, reject media via the remote proxy or explicitly allow the hostname in approved-only federation mode. Changes are enforced by both Node and Rust self-hosted federation verification, including cached site documents. The experimental independently authenticated Secure Net direct outbox/deliver/flush path respects the same host suspension and allowlist.

Added Site admin > Site rules & safety and public /rules. The owner-only settings preserve the stricter Docker OPEN_REGISTRATION=false and FEDERATION=false operator switches. Site moderation never claims to decrypt private messages, censor another independent site or change Secure Net protocol governance.

Improved Secure Net SNIP forum notes to distinguish merged PRs from declined/withdrawn PRs and link to the actual available GitHub reason or PR author's stated purpose. Notes explicitly separate merging code from adopting a protocol standard, and never invent a maintainer rationale.

Added a visible authorised-device Sync now control so default-server administrators can create, close and sign missing encrypted SNIP threads, including SNIP-0007 and SNIP-0008, without impersonating a device from the backend. Server-side code does not forge forum messages; the administrator must open and unlock Commonveil.

Documented local governance, domain moderation, security boundaries and the Docker/operator configuration in docs/SITE_POLICY.md and docs/SNIP_FORUM.md. Added tests for site owner/admin access, domain validation and transport enforcement across two independent self-hosted Node installations.

New Docker installations now mark the operator's setup-code account as the site owner. Existing Docker operators can assign or transfer ownership from the privileged container console with commonveil-server make-owner <username>, which is not a web API and is tested to maintain a single owner. The public /rules page is included in the sitemap and has source-linked hosting documentation.

releases.title: Secure Net SNIP proposals forum reconciliation and GitHub merge tracking
notes: The default community server SNIP proposals forum now creates missing threads for GitHub SNIP files and tracks whether a proposal file has reached the Secure Net default branch. A merge locks the discussion thread with a signed notice, but the message explicitly states that merging code is not accepting or ratifying a standard.

Existing Secure Net proposals SNIP-0001 through SNIP-0008 are eligible for reconciliation, including the missing 0007 and 0008. Posts and locks are still performed only by an authorised Commonveil admin device with the correct encryption keys, not by a backend pretending to be a human sender.

The forum checks soon after the authorised admin opens their app, every five minutes while visible, and on focus/connection restoration. The server retains GitHub response caching, fails closed on stale data, respects manually locked threads and uses stable post IDs to prevent duplicate forum posts.

The self-hosted Rust SNIP status implementation and hosted TypeScript functions use consistent merge state semantics. Tests cover open proposals, merged-but-still-draft proposals, closing without merge, duplicate IDs, unauthorised users and an unavailable GitHub API.

No private server encryption keys, Commonveil historical messages, Secure Net protocol signatures, experimental relay settings or live account-migration behaviour were changed. The existing stable Docker latest was not moved.

releases.title: Experimental independent Secure Net inbox, outbox and sealed site transport
notes: Introduced a separate, explicitly disabled-by-default Secure Net CVP-019 direct-message trial within the self-hosted Rust server. It is not built on Commonveil accounts, rooms or original version 1 federation and cannot access their private messages.

The experimental module verifies independently signed CVP-017 actor documents, manually pins trusted remote site public keys, issues high-entropy site-local actor credentials, validates recipient device lists and signed public X25519/ML-KEM-768 prekeys, and consumes one-time keys atomically.

Added actor-authenticated POST /cvp/v2/outbox, signed and hybrid post-quantum sealed POST /cvp/v2/deliver, recipient GET /cvp/v2/mailbox, acknowledgements, pending remote queue, operator-triggered flush, limited actor discovery and a manually pinned experimental site document. SQLite persists queued opaque ciphertext, delivery acknowledgements and replay nonces across server restarts.

Verified independent-actor access controls, malformed messages, wrong and missing site signatures, post-quantum sealing, recipient isolation, one-time prekey consumption and replay rejection. A two-server Rust HTTP integration test with separate databases exercises a signed and sealed remote delivery and its encrypted acknowledgement. It does not represent two independent third-party implementations or a fully decrypted end-to-end chat.

Added Docker variables EXPERIMENTAL_SECURE_NET_RELAY=false and SECURE_NET_RELAY_ADMIN=, with CI checks preserving the disabled and unset defaults. The relay can only be enabled by an operator on an isolated, disposable test instance.

Published detailed docs/SECURE_NET_RELAY.md endpoint descriptions and updated the public protocol guidance. No production CVP-019 capability advertisement, automatic discovery, full group/public messaging, independently reviewed key security, history migration or live inbox cutover is enabled. The hosted Commonveil site keeps the relay disabled and its original messaging unchanged.

releases.title: Secure Net as a standalone protocol: application integration and interoperability guidance
notes: Pinned the self-hosted Commonveil Rust server, client and patched OpenMLS dependencies to the latest CI-passing independent Secure Net draft revision e6128f2, including a private KEM-verifier snapshot and atomic-consume contract. The real Commonveil site does not expose this in-development KEM possession proof as a live API.

Added a public /secure-net developer page, a home-page introduction and Settings guidance explaining that Commonveil is Secure Net's first application, not the protocol owner or mandatory relay. Any compatible site or app can implement the independently governed protocol and its inbox/outbox communication model.

Published a third-party integration guide covering independent actor/device keys, authenticated client outbox, CVP-015 sealed site-to-site delivery, recipient mailbox, acknowledgements, metadata leakage and test obligations. The separate Commonveil version 1 federation document now explicitly identifies itself as a product-specific compatibility layer, not generic CVP-019.

The self-hosted Docker image now carries a label identifying it as a Commonveil application rather than a generic CVP-019 relay. GitHub CI checks this and checks both unreviewed migration gates remain off, with the exact Secure Net commit pinned consistently in Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock.

Added independent-protocol regression tests for developer docs, public route and Docker safety. The hosted site does not advertise full third-party Secure Net delivery or account portability until independently deployed implementations and human security reviewers verify them.

Existing messaging, user keys, Commonveil version 1 federation, private histories and inbox routes remain unchanged. Secure Net's publicly reviewed specifications and SNIPs, not a Commonveil release, determine new wire-protocol rules.

releases.title: Secure Net recipient consent foundation, disabled by default
notes: Aligned Commonveil Rust server/client and pinned Docker dependencies with Secure Net draft fe44f0d, including independent hybrid recipient request/grant records and an experimental KEM possession verifier in the shared protocol library.

Added strictly experimental self-hosted destination endpoints to verify, store and retrieve a receiving device’s hybrid-signed public MLKEM768-P256 key request and the identity owner’s separate hybrid-signed grant. A separate SQLite table stores only the exact validated signed public records; changes conflict, retries are idempotent, restart recovery works and abort deletes records.

Added an explicit EXPERIMENTAL_RECIPIENT_CONSENT environment gate, which also requires the existing EXPERIMENTAL_TRANSFER_STAGING=true flag. Both default to false in Docker Compose and operator examples. Docker CI checks both switches are off by default and the image’s Secure Net commit matches the Rust lockfile.

Added tests for independent recipient and actor signatures, wrong identity, forged grant, incomplete ciphertext, cross-stage replay, expiry, unauthorised stage token, immutable retries, server restart, cancellation and separate environment gating.

The prototype shared KEM challenge/response is not exposed as a Commonveil network endpoint because its in-memory nonce cannot yet provide crash-safe replay protection. Signed recipient consent is not KEM private-key possession, account binding, user history import, post-quantum history key exchange, inbox redirection or a live migration.

The hosted website gains accurate read-only readiness guidance while existing messaging, private keys, contacts, accounts and message routes remain unchanged. This work remains an unapproved, unaudited protocol draft; stable Docker latest is not automatically advanced.

releases.title: Shared Secure Net hybrid reconciliation and browser interoperability
notes: Updated the self-hosted Rust and Docker Secure Net pin from draft 12ab6f3 to the CI-passing e82fd9e reconciliation verifier. All Rust core, server and OpenMLS patch references move together under Cargo.lock.

Commonveil no longer duplicates provisional transfer.reconcile signature and schema verification: the disabled test-only Rust staging service now delegates owner-hybrid signatures, actor, stage, destination, challenge, archive root and signed report digest checks to the independent Secure Net crate.

Experimental encrypted-report staging now rejects missing CVRPT v1 headers, unsupported versions and invalid sizes using Secure Net shared report framing and digest checks. Old draft reports without a header must be discarded and re-staged on a private test instance.

Added client-side report commitment and associated-data helpers, with independent conformance tests against Secure Net synthetic fixtures and real AES-256-GCM encrypt/decrypt/tampering checks. Keys remain non-extractable and are never shared or enrolled by this feature.

Docker CI builds carry the exact pinned Secure Net revision in image labels and tests it against Cargo.lock. The only permitted development preview remains :edge; production :latest and normal user data remain untouched by experimental code.

The published Commonveil site only updates read-only Protocol identity guidance. No live account binding, key export, private history import, session rotation, source deletion, inbox redirection or protocol feature advertisement has been enabled.

releases.title: Secure Net draft integration and self-hosted Docker safety checks
notes: Pinned the self-hosted Rust server, Rust browser client core and the OpenMLS forks to the same tested experimental Secure Net SNIP-0007 revision. The destination staging service now verifies transfer intents and canonical ciphertext manifests using Secure Net’s Rust transfer helpers.

Updated Commonveil’s Protocol identity Settings to explain the independent actor model and the difference between read-only verification, disabled development staging and an actual migration. Destination compatibility checks do not import or move accounts.

The self-hosted Docker image records the pinned Secure Net source commit in an OCI label when built by the release workflow. Docker Compose keeps experimental staging disabled by default and CI checks that default and the pinned lockfile.

The JavaScript browser and hosted backend continue using the frozen Secure Net 0.5.0 compatibility implementation for existing encrypted messages. No live cryptography, account authentication, stored conversations or inbox routes are replaced by experimental migration routines.

Experimental transfer and reconciliation remain unaudited, disabled and not advertised as production CVP features. Full actor/account binding, private-history import, post-quantum recipient key handover, interop cutover and independent security review remain future milestones.

Fixed the Rust self-hosted voice-ticket response to include coturn REST relay credentials where configured, matching the Node.js reference server. Docker Compose now passes optional VOICE_TURN_URLS and VOICE_TURN_SECRET securely to the Rust server; a missing or invalid pair leaves direct calls unchanged.

GitHub CI now publishes opt-in :edge Docker app and updater images only after the website, Rust, WASM and image tests succeed. Stable :latest and numbered images are never changed by preview builds. Experimental images must not be run with production account data.

releases.title: Experimental migration: encrypted reconciliation report staging
notes: Extended the disabled self-hosted Rust migration destination to require a staged, bounded reconciliation report before it accepts the owner's separately signed report hash. The server re-hashes the private report and previously staged archive chunks under a transaction.

Added bearer-authorised opaque report upload and retrieval, idempotent identical retries, rejection of corruption or conflicting uploads, status visibility and deletion on abort. No decryption keys are stored on the server.

Added an experimental browser WebCrypto AES-256-GCM helper using an already authorised non-extractable device key. Authenticated associated data binds the independent actor, stage, destination, ciphertext root and recipient-device ID. It never exports or silently enrols a new device key.

The host cannot prove arbitrary uploaded bytes are encrypted, and a signed reconciliation statement does not prove successful message import, a zero-knowledge proof or permission to switch inbox routing.

This remains development-source-only, unadvertised and disabled by default. No live deployment, production image, source account or federation routing is changed. Added Rust server and client encryption tests.

Added a staged-only Rust HTTP test with two independent destination servers, confirming the same user-owned actor can prepare on B and C without either host issuing the identity, rejecting wrong-site signatures and crossed bearer tokens. This is not actual mailbox or account migration.

releases.title: Experimental migration: independent owner-signed reconciliation
notes: Added an owner-signed, stage-bound reconciliation statement to the experimental Rust-only destination service. The actor must be independently held and hybrid-signed with Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65, with no Commonveil identity-issuer requirement.

The staging server accepts a reconciliation statement only after all encrypted chunks are staged and the stored ciphertext is rehashed against its signed manifest. The statement binds the actor, stage, destination, root commitment, random per-stage challenge and a digest of a separately encrypted client report.

Strict validation rejects unsigned metadata, forged or mismatched statements, expired statements, corrupted ciphertext and conflicting retries. Identical retries are safe, and the bearer-authorised signed receipt is recoverable after Rust process restart.

Recording a client statement is not proof that the client decrypted private history, an audited zero-knowledge proof, an account import or a signed cutover. No message routes, account binding, existing encrypted histories, devices, or source data are changed.

This is source-only experimental work, disabled by default and unadvertised in production. Added three Rust unit tests and one live-HTTP integration test, updated safe test-only operator documentation, and kept the protocol wire migration incomplete pending independent review.

releases.title: Private-test foundation for independently owned account transfers
notes: The self-hosted Rust server now contains an opt-in, test-only destination service for holding already encrypted account-transfer chunks. No Commonveil account is required to issue a Secure Net actor identity.
It verifies one-use challenges and hybrid Ed25519/ML-DSA-65 signatures for an independently owned actor, retains monotonic transfer sequences, and stages ciphertext in a private SQLite database.

Transfer staging can recover after a server restart, report missing ciphertext, accept identical retries, reject corrupted chunks, and cancel without changing existing accounts, contacts, keys or message routing.

The endpoints are completely disabled by default and have strict size and time limits; this is not an actual account import, zero-knowledge proof, mailbox migration, deletion or source-offline recovery.
Added Rust unit and HTTP integration tests, operator documentation and a disabled Docker Compose setting. Full migration, interop tests and independent security review remain outstanding.

releases.title: Fix: Commonveil blank screen caused by Trusted Types clash
notes: Fixed the published website rendering a blank screen across the homepage, login and app routes. The voice-call diagnostics panel imported react-hot-toast, whose Goober CSS styling engine wrote directly to innerHTML during module initialization. Strict Trusted Types rejected the operation and prevented the whole JavaScript application from loading.
Replaced the two call-diagnostics toast notifications with the existing Commonveil Radix-based toast system. Copy success and clipboard-permission error messages remain visible in calls.
Added a production-bundle check rejecting Goober's unsafe style injector so this startup regression fails CI rather than reaching the public site.

Preserved the existing Content Security Policy and Trusted Types requirements. No security policy downgrades, authentication changes, encryption key changes, account resets, database migrations or protocol wire changes.
Verified the built homepage, login page and unauthenticated /app redirect in a Chromium browser with the production Content Security Policy enabled.

releases.title: Protocol identity: your actor, checked; another site, checked
notes: New Settings section, Protocol identity, showing this account's Secure Net actor (CVP-017): handle, actor id, fingerprint, key type, devices, version, and whether it verifies. The check runs in your browser against Secure Net's own rules rather than trusting what the site serves.

You can paste or choose an actor document made with any compatible application and have it checked here: the hybrid signature, an id that must be the account key's id, the signed device list, and a seq that never goes backwards, because this browser remembers the highest it has accepted. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is saved to your account.

Attaching an outside actor to your account stays off. It would need a fresh server challenge signed by that actor's key and by one of your certified devices, with replay protection and cross-instance tests. None of that is built, so the screen only reads, and no document is ever treated as proof of ownership.

A move to another site can now be prepared: the destination's public site document is fetched over HTTPS with a strict address guard (public names only, no redirects, reply capped) and its capabilities are listed one by one, including whether it serves actor documents. Nothing is moved, deleted or switched over.

Secure Net is described as it is: a neutral transport between sites, an inbox, an outbox and a relay, not an issuer of identities. No zero-knowledge proof is claimed: verification is ordinary hybrid signature checking.
Encryption, message routing and stored data are unchanged. No keys are stored on the server.

The destination checklist treats missing post-quantum relay keys, independent inbox and outbox endpoints, or versioned transfer support as blockers. No destination is automatically trusted for migration.

releases.title: Experimental encrypted identity archive preview
notes: Added a read-only identity archive tool under Settings that exports accessible conversations and contact references as a file protected by AES-256-GCM and signed using both Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65.
An archive can be independently checked and unlocked in the browser; only encrypted archive files persist in browser storage. Decrypted previews remain in memory while the screen is open.
This is not yet a portable account move. Existing DMs, site identity, credentials, membership rights, attachments and mailbox routing cannot be transferred with this preview.

Restored the independent Secure Net JavaScript compatibility package unchanged. Proposals for actual identity migration, inbox/outbox handover and audited privacy proofs are tracked in Secure Net draft SNIP-0007.
No authentication keys, federation endpoints, stored user messages or Rust server behaviour are changed by this release.

releases.title: Fix: push notifications blocked by unsupported edge redirect mode
notes: Fixed the actual reason push tests and automatic Web Push delivery failed on the hosted site: the Base44 edge runtime rejected redirect:error before making any outgoing HTTP request. All Web Push requests now use its supported manual mode.
An HTTP redirect from a push service is explicitly refused, never followed, so signed notifications cannot be redirected to arbitrary destinations.
Corrected the public Google connectivity diagnostic to use the same supported mode. It can now distinguish a genuine network failure from this runtime option error.
Applied the same safe redirect handling to Commonveil’s hosted federation transport, where the unsupported option could also prevent sites communicating.

All existing browser subscriptions, private encryption keys, muted-channel preferences and accounts are preserved. This release also removes the temporary outbound-network diagnostic endpoint used to identify the problem.
No configuration change is required for the Rust self-hosted server, which does not use the affected edge fetch API.

releases.title: Trace failed push connections safely
notes: Test notifications now distinguish a failure specific to the signed Web Push request from a failure to contact Google’s public push host at all. If a test fails with a network error, Commonveil checks the public Firebase Cloud Messaging host without transmitting the browser’s subscription, identifiers or keys.
New safe diagnostic categories distinguish network permissions, DNS, TLS, connection failure, invalid request setup and unclassified errors. They do not expose private URLs or raw exception messages.

These diagnostics help establish whether the hosted server’s outgoing network access must be fixed or whether the Web Push request itself needs repair. They do not claim a notification was received just because the server attempted to send it.
Fixed strict Rust lint warnings introduced by earlier push-notification changes. The Rust build and parity checks are also run by GitHub CI before a self-hosted release is considered fully verified.
No accounts, encryption keys, Web Push subscriptions or local notification preferences are reset by this update.

releases.title: Push tests now explain why they fail
notes: The test notification screen now reports whether the push service rejected the request (including its safe HTTP status code), a network request timed out, encryption could not be prepared, or the server could not connect. Before, every failure looked the same.
A failed test now reports the actual result straight away rather than leaving you checking for a notification that the server never sent successfully.

If the push service accepts a test but your browser does not show it, Commonveil no longer assumes the browser is blocking it. It explains that the failure could be anywhere between the push service and the device.
The diagnostics are specific to the device that requested the test and contain no browser push address, keys, message contents or identifiable notification metadata.
For people who self-host Commonveil, the Rust backend returns the same safe diagnostic categories. No additional configuration is required.

releases.title: Fix: push notification tests, delivery diagnostics, and server alerts
notes: Push notification tests now target the browser you are using, rather than all your devices. If the push service rejects a test, Commonveil reports the safe HTTP status code so the problem can be investigated.

When a push service fails or rejects a notification, Commonveil records only safe delivery outcomes, counts and HTTP status codes. It never logs message contents, browser push addresses or private keys, and a failed delivery does not start the usual 20-second cooldown.

Direct and group conversation messages still trigger background notifications. Channel messages and @mentions can now trigger generic alerts as well. Each browser follows its own All messages, Only @mentions or Nothing setting when deciding what to show.

Channel messages remain end-to-end encrypted. To route a mention when the app is closed, the sender shares only the IDs of the targeted accounts or roles with the server, never the words. This additional metadata is explained in the Help Centre and threat model.
Channel push fanout is initially limited to 200 server members per message. Larger communities need a queued notification service before every member can be guaranteed a background alert.
For people running a self-hosted site: no settings change is needed. Update the Rust server as normal once the new Docker image is available.

releases.title: Getting the app's encryption code ready to move to Rust
notes: Behind the scenes, Commonveil now builds the encryption code for your browser from Rust, as WebAssembly. Your browser still runs today's code: this release adds the Rust build and checks it.

Every change to Commonveil now checks that the Rust build and today's code agree on the building blocks of its encryption (keys, signatures and sealing), so the later move can be checked step by step.
Base44 updated the library the hosted site's app uses to talk to it (Base44's SDK, version 0.8.63), and this release includes that update.
Nothing changes for people using Commonveil.
For people who run a site: there's nothing to do, and the updater offers 0.24.3 as usual.

releases.title: Keeping the hosted site's server code deployable on Base44
notes: Base44, which runs the hosted site's server code, now refuses code that works out the name of a library while it runs. One part of the hosted site did that, as a fallback used only by our tests, so Base44 would have refused the hosted site's next update. That part now names its library directly, and a new check stops this from coming back.
This release also redeploys all of the hosted site's server functions, so every earlier fix to them is sure to be in place there.
Nothing changes in how Commonveil works or what it keeps: sealing between sites works exactly as before, and the hosted site still won't talk in the clear to a site that expects sealing.
For people who run a site: there's nothing to do. Self-hosted sites run the Rust server, which this doesn't touch, and the updater offers 0.24.2 as usual.

releases.title: Fix: files from conversations and servers on other sites wouldn't open
notes: Pictures, voice messages and other files sent in a conversation or server hosted on another self-hosted Commonveil site now open and download as they should. Before, they showed as no longer available, because the app asked your site for a file without saying where it was posted, and your site couldn't tell which other site held it.
The app now names the conversation or channel when it asks for a file, so your site passes the request to the right place. Files stay encrypted end to end throughout: neither site can read them.
Forwarding a file that came from another site works now too, for the same reason.

A site answering for its own conversations can't hand your app links for files posted anywhere else, and a file can't be made to appear under someone else's message, even by a message that names its parts.
Conversations and servers hosted on the Base44 site don't share files with other sites yet, so those files still can't be opened from a self-hosted site; the app now says so plainly.
For people who run a site: update as usual (the updater offers 0.24.1); there's nothing to change in your settings.

releases.title: Self-hosted sites now run on a server written in Rust
notes: Self-hosted Commonveil sites now run on a new server written in Rust, in place of the Node.js one. It does what the old server did: the same features, the same answers to the app, and the same end-to-end encryption, which still happens on your devices.
Nothing changes for people using a site. You stay signed in, your conversations, servers, files and settings are where they were, and other sites still recognise yours.

Before the switch, every part of the new server was run side by side with the old one on the same requests, and every answer had to match, including two sites talking to each other with one on each server. A site made by the old server was also copied and carried on by the new one, to check that nothing is lost in the move.

For people who run a site: the Docker image no longer contains Node.js. It uses the data volume, the settings and the site's keys as they are, so there is nothing to change. Admin commands now start with docker compose exec app commonveil-server (instead of node server/index.mjs), for example docker compose exec app commonveil-server setup-code.

The updater, the container that installs updates, is written in Rust too. The one you have keeps working; to move it to the new one, run docker compose pull updater && docker compose up -d updater once.
Sites on a local network with their own certificate authority can name it with the new EXTRA_CA_CERTS setting. NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, which such sites set before, still works.
The hosted site, commonveil.online, is not changed by this release.

releases.title: Fix: the app showed a blank page after signing in
notes: Fixed a mistake in 0.23.0 that made the app show a blank page straight after "Checking your keys", for everyone signed in. No messages, keys or accounts were affected: the app stopped before it showed anything.

The cause was two lines of the new experimental protocol code placed above the code they depend on. A new check now runs on every change and fails if any part of the app uses something before it is defined.
The app, the new Settings switch and turning the experimental layer on have now been checked in a real browser.

releases.title: A first step onto the Secure Net protocol (experimental), and a forum for protocol proposals
notes: Commonveil now carries the new Secure Net protocol (0.5.0) and takes its first step onto it. It is off unless you turn it on: Settings, Devices and keys, Experimental: Secure Net protocol.

With it on for both people, a direct message is sealed a second time under a one-off key. That key goes only to the devices linked at that moment, over post-quantum sessions (X25519 with ML-KEM-768), so someone who later gets hold of an account's keys or recovery phrase still can't read it.
It adds to the protection messages already have and never replaces it. Messages to people who haven't turned it on go exactly as before, and everything already sent stays readable.
Turning it on gives your account a protocol identity: a quantum-resistant key and the handle @username@site.

Limits for now: direct messages only (not groups, servers, edits, reactions or scheduled messages); a device added later can't read messages sent with it before; it can't be used together with a passcode lock; and it works within one site.
It is labelled experimental because the protocol has not had an independent security review yet. docs/SECURE_NET_LAYER.md says exactly what it does and what the site can see.
Self-hosted sites get the same feature with this update; there is nothing new to configure.
New: the community server gets a forum, snip-proposals, with one thread for every Secure Net Improvement Proposal (SNIP) on GitHub. Anyone in the server can read the threads and reply.

Threads follow GitHub by themselves: a new proposal gets a thread, and a thread is closed with a note when its proposal is accepted, rejected, implemented, released or withdrawn, or its pull request is closed without merging.
Posts stay end-to-end encrypted, so the site can't write them. A community admin's app does it whenever they have Commonveil open, so changes on GitHub show up the next time an admin is online.
Only the site reads GitHub, and only its public list of proposals. Your device never contacts GitHub.
Self-hosted sites: this is off unless you set SNIP_FORUM=on (docs/SNIP_FORUM.md).

releases.title: A sealed, quantum-resistant relay between sites
notes: What one site sends another is now sealed for that site alone, so nothing in between can see who is writing to whom, which conversation, or what was asked: not the network, not a CDN or hosting platform, and not someone recording traffic to decrypt later.
The sealing is quantum-resistant: ML-KEM-768 together with a classical exchange, so it holds unless both are broken. Answers come back sealed too.
Sites sign what they send twice, with Ed25519 and the post-quantum ML-DSA-65. Both must check out.
A site that has started sealing can't be talked back down: other sites refuse it if its relay keys change or vanish, and refuse plain or singly-signed requests from it.
Communities' signed records (history, votes, results) can use quantum-resistant keys.
Your messages themselves were already quantum-resistant end to end. Still classical for now: the signatures your devices put on messages, and private voting tokens.
Built on Secure Net 0.3.1. Self-hosted sites pick this up by updating; nothing to configure.

releases.title: The hosted site can talk to self-hosted sites
notes: The hosted site now speaks the same protocol as self-hosted sites: people on either can find each other by address, start conversations, and read and reply, end-to-end encrypted, with each person's keys checked against their own key history.

Sites now tell each other where their protocol endpoints are in their site document, so a site that can only be reached under a path can take part. Self-hosted sites need this release to talk to the hosted site.
People from other sites never get an account on the hosted site: it keeps only what their own site shares about them, and they can't sign in there.
Not yet between the hosted site and others: calls and presence, files and pictures in conversations hosted elsewhere, and holding messages for a site that's down.
Self-hosted sites: new optional setting FEDERATION_PATH_PREFIX, for a site that can only be reached under a path.
Built on Secure Net 0.2.1.

releases.title: A full security review, and Secure Net
notes: All 24 findings from an independent security review are fixed, each with a test. docs/SECURITY_REVIEW.md lists them.
Disconnecting a device, changing your password or recovering your account now signs out every other session at once.
Adding a passkey, approving a new browser or replacing your owner key now needs proof it's you: one of your devices confirms it without asking, or you enter your password.
Removing a device now changes the keys of every community it could read, so it can't read anything new.
Self-hosted sites: the first admin needs a one-time setup code printed on the server, so a stranger can't claim a new site first. ADMIN_USERNAMES and email (SMTP) settings are gone.
Self-hosted sites: updates that fail no longer stay "Updating…", the updater won't go backwards unless you allow it, and backups are pruned by age.
Self-hosted sites no longer depend on Base44 in any way: the image builds and runs with nothing of theirs, and a check stops the build if that ever changes.
Talking to other sites is safer: a site's address is checked at the moment of connecting, and replies are cut off as soon as they're too big.

Commonveil is now built on Secure Net, our protocol as a separate library (github.com/Comutability/secure-net) that other apps and sites can use. It adds communities that approved sites can mirror and keep running if their home site goes down, structured debates and votes (public or secret) that can authorise changes, private tokens (RFC 9497), personas, consent capsules, and extension and theme manifests.

releases.title: Sign in your way, install the app, and private push notifications
notes: New accounts are a username and password, on every Commonveil site. No email needed.
Accounts made with an email before today still sign in with it, and can add a username and password, or a passkey, and then remove the email.
Joining asks you to confirm you're 16 or older. Accounts found to belong to someone younger are closed.
Terms of Use, in plain language, linked from sign-up and every page.
Install Commonveil as an app on your phone, tablet or computer: its own icon and window, opening straight to your messages, still this website with no app store.

Push notifications, off until you turn them on. They say only "New message", never who it's from, which conversation or what was said, so your phone and its push service keep no record. Tapping one opens the right conversation.
Better for screen readers and keyboards: a skip link in the app, clearer names for buttons and badges, and higher-contrast avatars.

Easier to find: every page that works without signing in has its own title, description and link preview, with a sitemap for search engines. The app is never indexed, and nor are invites, reset links or people's profiles.
New Help Centre article: installing the app. The notifications article now covers push.

releases.title: Offline mode
notes: Keep writing with no connection: each message is encrypted and signed on your device straight away, waits there, and goes out when you're back, showing the time you wrote it.
Offline mode in settings stops the app reaching the server until you turn it off. Everything you send in the meantime waits, already encrypted.
If something changed while you were away, a waiting message is marked "Not sent", with Send again or Delete.
Self-hosted sites hold messages for other sites they can't reach, and pass them on when they can, for up to a week.
A self-hosted site can run on a small computer with its own Wi-Fi, so people nearby can chat with no internet. The guide is in docs/OFFLINE.md and docs/SELF_HOSTING.md.
New Help Centre articles: offline mode, people on other sites, sign-in and recovery, and running your own site.

releases.title: Commonveil Identity
notes: On self-hosted sites, accounts are a username and password, with no email.
Sign in with a passkey, kept on one device or synced by a password manager.

A browser signing in for the first time is confirmed with a passkey, your recovery phrase or private key, or from a device you're already signed in on. Signed-in devices are listed in settings, where you can disconnect any of them.
Your private key is your recovery phrase written as one string: either proves the account is yours. Getting back in takes one of them, or a passkey.
Accounts made with an email still work, and are asked to add a passkey and confirm their phrase before email sign-in goes away.

releases.title: Run it yourself, and talk across sites
notes: Commonveil can run on your own hardware with Docker, without Base44: one install script, HTTPS included.
Self-hosted sites show admins when a new release is out, with an update button, and can update themselves automatically. Each update is backed up first and undone if it doesn't start.

Self-hosted sites talk to each other with the Commonveil Protocol: everyone has an address like @ann.chat.example.com that also opens their profile, and conversations and servers work across sites, still end-to-end encrypted.
Browse and join servers listed on other sites from Discover.
Profile pictures.
The message box grows with longer messages, and can be expanded.
The home page compares Commonveil with other privacy-focused chat apps.

releases.title: A tighter site, with release notes
notes: Guides, learning paths, the wiki and the blog have been removed, so the site is about Commonveil itself. Their old addresses now lead to the Help Centre.
Release notes for every version, from 0.1.0 onwards, on the site and as tags on GitHub.
The site's version is shown at the bottom of every page.
Commonveil is now free software, under the AGPL-3.0.

releases.title: Help Centre
notes: A Help Centre with an article for every feature: what it's for, how to use it and what it shares.
The complete guide on one page, to print or download, and as docs/USER_GUIDE.md on GitHub.
"How this works" links from settings pages to the right article.

releases.title: Scheduled tasks fixed
notes: Scheduled tasks now run reliably: scheduled messages, check-ins and self-destructing conversations every 5 minutes, disappearing messages every 30 minutes, and opt-in account deletion daily.
The self-destruct menu no longer lists "Off" twice.

releases.title: Send later, safety check-ins and self-destructing chats
notes: Send later: write now, deliver from a minute to a year ahead.
Safety check-ins: a message that sends itself unless you tap "I'm OK" in time.
Self-destructing conversations, deleted for everyone at a time you choose.
A privacy report showing everything the service holds about you, with a privacy checkup.
Quiet hours and focus for notifications, kept on your device.

releases.title: Names in moderation
notes: Reports and cases show the names of members who aren't in the member list, instead of "Member".

releases.title: Security audit and built-in moderation
notes: Fixes from a full security review: channel permissions, private channels, call membership checks and safer word matching.
Reports to a server's moderators, encrypted to them alone, and escalation to the Commonveil team.
Numbered cases, warnings with automatic steps, flood and raid protection, staff limits, temporary bans and message purges.

releases.title: Files, voice messages, events and more
notes: Encrypted files and voice messages.
A server's own emoji and stickers, AutoMod, threads and events.
Optional online status and typing, stage channels, and calls in conversations.

releases.title: Video and screen sharing
notes: Turn your camera on or share your screen in calls, with every video frame encrypted too.

releases.title: Polls, inbox and quick switcher
notes: Polls, every emoji as a reaction, an inbox for mentions and unread channels, saved messages, a quick switcher (Ctrl + K), server folders, private notes and forwarding.

releases.title: Calls recover from network drops
notes: Calls find a new route by themselves after a network drop.

releases.title: Calls survive a quick reconnect
notes: You keep your place in a call through a quick reconnect.

releases.title: Encrypted voice calls
notes: Peer-to-peer voice calls in voice channels, with signed connections and every audio frame encrypted with the channel's keys.

releases.title: Server settings fixes
notes: Server settings load correctly after a reload, a note about staff in member lists, and clearer text while waiting for keys.

releases.title: Servers and the community hub
notes: Encrypted servers with channels, roles, invites and Discover, the Commonveil Community server, and post-quantum hybrid keys, now live.

releases.title: Faster server updates
notes: Server changes are checked separately from messages.

releases.title: A new layout
notes: A server rail, channel list, chat, forums, tickets and settings, laid out like Discord.

releases.title: Who hands out keys
notes: Servers choose whether any member's app or only staff hand keys to newcomers.

releases.title: Post-quantum keys and encrypted servers
notes: Keys sealed with ML-KEM-768 and P-256 together, and the groundwork for encrypted servers.

releases.title: Checks after going live
notes: The live site was checked, and the security policy test fixed.

releases.title: Live, with updated privacy pages
notes: The new features were verified on the live site, and the Privacy and Security pages updated.

releases.title: Replies, reactions and a passcode lock
notes: Replies, reactions and edits; disappearing-message timers and group admins; alerts; message search on your device; a passcode lock; a download of your data; opt-in auto-delete; and site search.

releases.title: Timers, admins and security emails
notes: Disappearing messages, group admins, security emails, opt-in deletion of unused accounts and scheduled clean-up, on the server.

releases.title: Protocol version 2
notes: Fixes from a review of the encryption protocol, each member reading with their own access, and a staff tool for erasing what removed sign-ins left behind.

releases.title: Signed group changes
notes: Changes to groups need a device signature, membership can be paused, a stale-keys fix, and a browser test suite.

releases.title: The rebuild
notes: Commonveil rebuilt from scratch: end-to-end encrypted direct messages and groups, device linking, a 24-word recovery phrase and safety numbers.
The public site, with content brought over from the old one.
